title: The Same Wait
logline: For thirty-eight years one stretch of dry-zone scrub and rock on the south-east coast was kept by law for sportsmen to shoot in, while the ground across the river was kept for nothing to be shot at all; since 1938 the shooting ground has been the most watched wild country on the island. The film is made from inside a halted vehicle with a very long lens rested on the sill, doing exactly what a stalker did here a century ago: reading the ground, fixing on an animal, holding still. The texts say the drive in that posture has no colour of its own.
human_question: When I wait a long time, very still, for something I want to see, is there anything in the waiting itself that says what kind of wanting it is?

place.what_kind_of_place: A dry-zone coastal wilderness of thorn scrub, open grassy plains, shallow lagoons and seasonal waterholes, with bare gneiss inselbergs standing up out of the flat country to about ninety metres, bounded on one side by the sea and on the other by a sand-bedded river that runs almost dry in the drought. It is the oldest and most visited block of a national park, entered through one gate, crossed only by vehicle on sand and gravel tracks, and closed every evening at six. Nobody lives in it. What gives it its story is a line: in 1900 the government divided this country along the river, keeping the far bank as a sanctuary where nothing could be shot and reserving this bank for resident sportsmen to shoot in. In 1938 this bank became the national park. The ground, the animals and the tracks are the same ones; only the law on it changed.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: It is some of the most photogenic open country on the island and the film gives it the treatment it is usually denied: no drone (flying is prohibited in the park), no wide scenic sweep, only the compressed, heat-rippled world of a very long lens held from a stationary vehicle. Through six or eight hundred millimetres the plain turns into layers stacked on one another: a line of spotted deer, a band of shimmering air, a grey dome of rock floating above scrub. A raptor lifting off a dead tree with hard strokes and then gliding. Pug marks in the sand of a track in raking afternoon light. The dry river bed, pale sand between dark walls of forest. And at the end, the last light on the rock and whatever animal is on it, held in a frame that does not move for minutes. With the sound off it is a patient, beautiful wildlife film that never shows a person, and ends by turning round to show the instrument it was made with.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The light and the air, and the animals, none of it controlled. The film runs through one afternoon session, from the gate opening after midday into the last light before the six o'clock closing. The heat haze is thick at the start and thins as the sun drops; the rock faces go from grey to orange; the plains empty of shade. Animals appear and do not; the film waits. The camera itself does not travel within a shot: every frame is taken from a halted vehicle, and the only movement is a slow pan to follow something that moves. The one change the film makes on purpose is its last cut, a reverse angle onto the camera.
place.when_it_looks_best: The dry season, roughly June to August, late afternoon: water shrinks to a few holes, animals gather at them, the plains are pale and bare, and the haze makes the long lens stack the landscape into layers. The last forty minutes before the six o'clock closing give the warm light on the inselbergs. The park is normally closed for some weeks from September for the drought, so the window ends there. Monsoon greenery in the wet months would soften everything the film needs to look hard and bright.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: An afternoon in dry wild country seen entirely through a very long lens from a vehicle that never moves while it films. Heat haze over a plain. Tracks in sand. A bird of prey rising and gliding. A dry river with a far bank. A herd at a shrinking waterhole. A long, still wait for something to show itself, and then something does: an animal on a rock in the last warm light, held for a long time. Then one cut turns the camera round, and the viewer sees the lens resting on a bag on the door sill, pointing out at the rock, rested and steadied the way a rifle is. The piece has a beginning (the gate), a middle (the stalk and the wait) and a payoff (the sighting and the reveal of the instrument), and it resolves with no words needed.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same footage becomes a demonstration of the six occasional mental factors, and of why the texts refuse to give them a colour. The voice points only at what is visible. The tracks in the sand are what the texts call directing the mind onto an object and working it over: the stroke of a bell and its hum, the hawk beating up and then gliding, which the camera shows literally. The long wait is effort in the texts' own sense, not retreating until the thing begun is done, and the texts say it is mental, not bodily strength. The whole stalk runs on the wish to do, which the texts insist is not the sticking force that makes wanting. Then the history supplies the proof no argument could: on this very ground, for thirty-eight years, the same reading of tracks, the same stillness and the same wish to find the animal were aimed down a rifle, and since 1938 they have been aimed down lenses. Nothing in the posture changed. The texts say these factors are wholly good in a good mind and wholly bad in a bad one, and take their colour from what they join; the film cannot see what they joined, then or now, and says so. A second thread uses the texts on wanting to refuse the easy verdict: the texts' list of harms that greed can drive does not include killing, and the three things they do look at in any wanting (glad or flat, a reason attached or not, rising alone or pushed) are things no gazette, licence or lens can record.

sequence.on_screen: Early afternoon, the heat at its worst. From a halted vehicle just inside the gate, an 800 mm frame straight down the sand track: the track, a band of trembling air, grey scrub, and far off a dome of bare rock that seems to float. Nothing moves except the air. Held for twenty seconds.
sequence.voice: In 1900 the government drew a line across this country along a river. The far side was made a sanctuary, where nothing could be shot. This side, the side the camera is on, was reserved for resident sportsmen to shoot in. It stayed that way for thirty-eight years. It is the same ground now. Only the law on it has changed, twice.

sequence.on_screen: Tracks. A long lens tilted down at the sand beside the vehicle in raking afternoon light: pug marks crossing the wheel ruts, each toe a small crater with a shadow in it. Then a slow pan along them until they leave the track and vanish into scrub. The camera stays where it is.
sequence.voice: Anyone who wanted to find an animal here, then or now, had to do two things with the mind. Bring it onto something, a print in the sand, and then stay with it, work it over, follow it. The texts taught in this series name those two and say they arise together, like the stroke of a bell and the hum that goes on after it. They are in the mind of whoever is reading these tracks. The texts do not say whose, or why.

sequence.on_screen: A dead tree standing in the open. On it a bird of prey. It drops, beats hard, three or four heavy strokes, climbs, and then sets its wings and slides across the frame without a single beat, the lens panning to hold it until it leaves the haze.
sequence.voice: The older of the two texts uses exactly this picture. Directing the mind onto its object is a hawk beating its wings to climb into the sky. Staying with the object is the same hawk gliding, its wings still. And it says these factors, with four others, are found in good minds and bad alike: in a good mind wholly good, in a bad mind wholly bad. They have no colour of their own.

sequence.on_screen: The river in the dry season: a wide bed of pale sand with a few dark pools, a wall of forest on the far bank, a fallen trunk. The lens looks across, not along. Nothing crosses. A long hold on the far bank, where the sanctuary was.
sequence.voice: The far bank got a keeper a few years after it was declared. Henry Engelbrecht was a Boer prisoner of war who had refused the oath to the British crown and had not been sent home. The accounts of him that survive were written later and at second hand, and they disagree about the year he started and the year he died. They agree about why he was the man for it: he was a first-class shot and a good tracker. The skill that kept this bank was the skill being used on the other.

sequence.on_screen: A waterhole shrinking in a ring of cracked mud, a herd of spotted deer at the far edge, a buffalo lying in what is left of the water. The camera does not move for a full minute of screen time; the only change is a deer lifting its head. The sound is heat, insects, a distant peacock.
sequence.voice: Most of a stalk is this. The texts define effort as not falling back from the task, going on until what was begun is done. They are careful to say they mean a strength of mind, not of the body. And they do not call it a virtue. The same effort holds a good mind to its object and holds a bad one to its object, just as firmly. The wait before a shot and the wait before a photograph are the same wait.

sequence.on_screen: Late sun. The open plain going gold, long shadows of scrub, a line of deer moving across it in single file, the inselbergs behind them turning orange. Wide for the first time in the film, but still a long lens: the plain compressed into three bands of animals, grass and rock.
sequence.voice: In 1938 this bank became a national park and the shooting stopped. It is tempting to say that greed was shut out on that day. The text on wanting does not allow it. It lists the harmful acts that a mind rooted in wanting can drive, and killing is not on the list. What it looks for in any wanting is three things: whether it comes glad or flat, whether it carries a reason that says there is nothing wrong in it, whether it rises by itself or has to be pushed. A licence cannot record any of them. Neither can a law, and neither can this lens.

sequence.on_screen: The last warm light before six. On a low rock an animal, a leopard if the day gives one, otherwise whatever is there, lying still. The 800 mm frame holds it without moving for a long time. Then one cut: the reverse angle, from outside the vehicle, of the long lens resting on a bean bag on the door sill, pointing out at the rock. No face, no hands in frame. Then black, and the sound of an engine starting for the gate.
sequence.voice: Under all of it is one more thing, the wish to do: to find it, to see it. The texts insist it is not the force that makes a mind stick. Beside wanting, it works for wanting. Beside a mind turned against wanting, it works against it. They even say that, trained, it is what carries a person to the highest things they know of, which no camera can show. The lens is held the way a rifle is held: rested, steadied, pointed, still. Nothing in the posture says which way it leans.

concept_merge.why_together: C021 is the primary and carries almost every beat: the six occasional factors, which the Pradeepika says are found in both wholesome and unwholesome minds and become wholly wholesome or wholly unwholesome according to the mind they join [C021-P:L25]. This ground makes that sentence visible because its own history ran the same stalk under two opposite laws. C006 is the supporting concept and does a narrower, protective job. A film about a former shooting ground invites the verdict that the hunters were greedy and the watchers are not. C006 refuses that verdict on its own terms: the Pradeepika's list of the harmful courses of action that can be done with a greed-rooted mind names theft, sexual misconduct, false, divisive and idle speech, covetousness and wrong view, and does not name killing [C006-P:L54]; and what C006 does look for in any wanting is three dials, glad or neutral [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74], with or without a view that denies fault or consequence [C006-P:L33], unprompted or prompted [C006-P:L44] [C006-P:L58–L62], none of which is recorded in any document the ground has.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the colour of a drive is not in the drive, and not in the rule that governs it either. C021 alone would make a film about effort and attention; C006 alone would make a film about wanting. Together they show the same patient, skilled, wish-driven stalk, recorded first in a law that reserved shooting and then in a law that ended it, and they show that neither law, nor the posture, nor the camera can tell which of the mind's dials was set where. The voice ends on the wish to do because C021 says it is exactly the factor that can go either way [C021-P:L75] [C021-M:L27].

concept_links.why: The digest's first finding is that aiming, turning over, deciding, pushing on, being uplifted and wanting to do have no colour of their own: the Pradeepika says the occasional factors occur scattered through wholesome and unwholesome minds and are counted wholly wholesome with the one and wholly unwholesome with the other [C021-P:L25]. The film shows four of the six at work in a stalk and cites the texts' own images for them: initial application as the hawk beating up into the sky [C021-P:L33] and sustained application as the hawk gliding with still wings [C021-P:L41], the two arising together like a bell's stroke and its hum, not in sequence [C021-M:L11]; effort as not falling back until the thing begun is done, a strength of mind and not of body [C021-M:L19]; and desire-to-act as the wish to take up the object, not the force that makes the mind stick [C021-P:L69], in accord with greed in greed-accompanied minds and opposed to it in minds opposed to greed [C021-M:L27], and, developed, a base of success that helps suppress craving and leads towards absorption and liberation [C021-P:L75]. The location is where this is the only honest reading of the record: the same ground, the same reading of tracks and the same stillness served shooting under the 1900 reservation and watching since 1938. The digest's does_not_transfer lines bind the voice: effort is not called virtuous ('hard work is always virtuous' is refused), the watching is not called good or the old shooting bad on the strength of drive alone ('follow your passion' is refused), and desire itself is not made the enemy, since the source says the opposite about desire-to-act. Decision (adhimokkha) and rapture (pīti) are not used: the group's pilgrimage film already carries decision, and the digest flags the rapture physiology as traditional; nobody in this film is shown as uplifted.

C006 is how the eight greed-rooted minds arise, and in this film it guards the primary rather than accusing anyone. The Pradeepika's list of the seven harmful courses of action that can be done through greed does not include killing [C006-P:L54], so the film cannot, on its own texts, call the shooting that happened here greed, and it says so. What C006 does look for is three dials: joy on meeting a pleasing object or neutral feeling [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L74], a view that denies consequences or that there is any fault in the act [C006-P:L33], and whether the mind rises sharply by itself or has to be urged on by others or by oneself [C006-P:L44] [C006-P:L58–L62]. The film's point is that a reservation, a licence, a national park ordinance and a camera record none of them. The digest's does_not_transfer lines apply directly: the voice never offers the stillness of the watching as proof of a good mind ('calm means good' is refused, the Margaya ranking neutral greed above joyful [C006-M:L19]); it never implies that the 1938 law made anyone's wanting lighter ('guilt-free pleasure' is refused); and wrong view is never mapped onto any community. The group's hill-station film has already used C006's list of favouring conditions and the full ranking in its voice, so this film keeps to the three dials and the course-of-action list.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That effort, attention, patience and the wish to do something are the working parts of any purposeful moment, and that on the texts' account none of them is good or bad in itself: they take the colour of whatever they serve. The proof is on screen and needs no belief. This ground was divided by law in 1900 into a shooting reserve and a sanctuary, and the shooting reserve became the most visited wild country on the island; the stalk the camera performs is the stalk the law once licensed, and the only visible difference is the instrument. A second, quieter understanding: that the texts on wanting do not hand out the verdict a viewer expects, and that the things which would settle it are not the kind of thing a document or a camera holds.
what_must_be_real: Every animal, track and waterhole as found on the day; nothing baited, called, chased or positioned, and no vehicle driven to cut an animal off for the shot. The film follows the park's rules exactly, which is part of its argument: the camera stays in the vehicle and on the track, and the session ends at the closing hour. No person is framed as a character or shown with a readable face, including drivers, trackers, rangers, other visitors and the crew; the reverse shot at the end shows the lens, the bag and the sill only. The history in the voice is limited to what the written record supports and says where the accounts disagree. If the day gives no leopard, the payoff is whatever animal is there, or an empty rock, and the voice is unchanged.
position_hint: Mid-group in GRP-02: after the films that establish what wanting is and how its dials work, and before the films that ask how the same act can have different aims. This is the film that says the drive under any wanting has no colour of its own, which the rest of the group's arguments rely on. It should not sit next to the group's other animal films (the whale grounds and the elephant nursery, both proposed) if those are kept.
risks: Charging the sportsmen of 1900 to 1938 with greed. The texts do not put killing on greed's list, the brief forbids framing any hunter as wanting, and the voice says outright that it cannot see which dial any of them had set. Nothing in the film may imply they were worse people than today's visitors, or better.

Charging today's visitors, drivers or trackers with greed, or praising them for watching instead of shooting. 'Calm means good' is on C006's does_not_transfer list, and C021's says effort and drive guarantee nothing. The watchers are never shown as faces, never counted, and never contrasted morally with anyone.

The 2004 tsunami. The coastal part of this block was struck, people died there, and a memorial stands on the shore. It is out of frame and out of the voice entirely (no bereavement or remembrance register), and the coastal stretch around it is not used even as landscape.

Henry Engelbrecht's grave. His gravestone, erected by the sportsmen's society, is the clearest early document of his service, but a grave is remembrance; it is used in research only and never filmed or quoted.

Living communities. The seasonal fishing camp on this block's shore, the pilgrim traffic in the neighbouring blocks, and the villages at the park edge are not subjects and are not filmed or named. The film does not enter any question of who may use the park, grazing, encroachment or the jeep trade.

The 'rifle and lens' rhyme turning into a pun or a cute analogy. It must stay a documented fact about this ground (it was reserved for shooting, and it is now the most watched block) with the posture shown once, at the end, and not played for irony.

Letting the history become a conservation success story. 'Hunters became protectors' is a verdict about minds the film cannot see; the voice records two laws and one ground and leaves the colour undecided, which is what the primary concept says.
Narrating animals as having states of mind. The leopard is not 'wary', the deer are not 'afraid'. They are filmed and not interpreted.
Kamma as fate or desert, in either direction: nothing about the animals shot here, or the animals living here now, is narrated as deserved or as a reward.

Traditional teaching narrated as fact: the texts' hawk and bell are images the texts use, spoken as the texts' images; the rapture physiology is not used at all. The voice's mention of what the wish to do can lead to is marked as what the texts say, and as something no shot shows.

Repetition inside the group. Two other GRP-02 films are proposed with animals (whale grounds; an elephant capture ground and a calf nursery), and one other C021-primary film is proposed in a protected forest. This film must not use feeding, captures, archival photographs, a campaign story or the 'downhill boat' image, all of which belong to those films.
drop_if: The Department of Wildlife Conservation will not permit filming in the block, or will not allow a long-lens rig rested on a stationary vehicle on the public tracks.

Further research shows that this block was not in fact the resident sportsmen's shooting reserve before 1938 (for example, if the reservation lay elsewhere and the IUCN directory's account is mistaken). The whole film rests on that fact.

The group review judges three animal films, or two films about taking animals giving way to protecting them, to be a run; in that case this film or the elephant film should go, not both kept with softened treatments.
The park's closure dates or crowding in the dry season make a quiet, unhurried afternoon session on the tracks impossible to film without other vehicles in every frame.

connections.note: Proposed in the GRP-02 selection (still being written): a former elephant capture ground and a nursery for orphaned calves, built on one gesture, a bottle of milk held to a wild calf, made for two aims seventy years apart. Both films sit on the change from taking wild animals to protecting them, and that is the pair's weakness. They divide the ground this way: that film is about the aim of a gesture (C005) and pays off on a cut from an archival photograph; this one is about the drive under any aim (C021), uses no archive, shows no feeding or capture, and pays off on a reverse angle onto the camera.

Proposed in the GRP-02 selection: the other C021-primary film, a rainforest whose logging was stopped after a campaign, carried by the texts' image of effort as a boat carried downstream and good done as a load carried uphill. The same conservation society that grew out of this film's sportsmen's club appears in that story, so this film does not name the society's later names in its voice and does not use the boat image. Monsoon, canopy and a walked track there; dry season, heat haze and a camera that never leaves a halted vehicle here.

Proposed in the GRP-02 selection: whale-watching grounds and a shipping lane off the south coast, the group's water-borne film. Both look at animals through lenses. That film puts its charge on a regulation and a trade route and is filmed from a boat with a high drone at dawn; this one puts no charge on anyone, uses no drone, and is filmed from land into the last light.

The group's pilgrimage-shrine film (written) closes on the same C021 finding from the other side, the wish to build as not itself the sticking force, and uses the texts' decision factor on a colonial writer's firm footnote. This film takes the wish to do as its whole subject rather than its coda, and leaves decision alone. Noon, a locked frame and a straight-down drone there; dusk, an 800 mm lens and no drone here.

The group's hill-station film (written) uses C006's conditions for the sharp, unprompted mind, weather among them, and the Margaya's full ranking. This film uses C006 differently, for the course-of-action list and the three dials as things a document cannot record, and avoids the conditions list and the ranking in its voice. Frost, dawn and macro there; heat, dusk and extreme telephoto here.

Another group's film: a granite lighthouse on a reef in open sea off this same south-east coast, whose record describes the land behind the beach as a protected wilderness. The two films share a coast and nothing else: a light kept for sailors it never sees there, a line drawn through wild country here. Neither shows the other's site.

Another group's film on a small offshore marine national park, built on its staff shutting it down for the monsoon. The only other national park on the slate; a reef, a boardwalk and a closing-up there, a dry-zone plain, a legal line and a stalk here.

selection.reason: Kept on the blind GRP-02 selection's proposal after testing both halves. The story half held, and got sharper under checking: the proposal described a hunters' society whose reserve became a sanctuary, but the IUCN protected-areas directory of 1990 (drawing on the society's own 75th-anniversary history) records that Block I itself, the block the public now visits, was the Resident Sportsmen's Shooting Reserve from 1900, while the 1900 sanctuary was the neighbouring block across the river. So the most watched ground on the island is the ground once kept for shooting, which is C021's claim, that a drive takes the colour of what it serves, as a documented fact about one place. The proposal's C006 reading (sport killing licensed, commercial killing banned, as a view that lightens a wanting) was dropped, because the Pradeepika's list of courses of action done through greed does not include killing; C006 is used instead to refuse the verdict. The place half is not in doubt. The weaknesses are stated in the review note: a third animal film in the group, a shared 'taking to protecting' arc with the elephant film, and a keeper whose dates no two sources agree on.

review.note: This record's body was replaced in full on 2026-09-26 in the blind GRP-02 re-selection, written without reading the previous body. The previous status was already pending, so no confirmation or rejection has been reset, but under standing decision 9 any earlier reading of this record no longer applies. The concepts are unchanged (C021 primary, C006 supporting). The location, proposed by Claude, is Block I of the national park on the south-east coast, entered by its main gate, which was the blind selection's proposal; it was tested and kept. The key fact under the film is from the IUCN protected-areas directory of 1990, which rests on T. W. Hoffmann's 1969 history of the wildlife society in Loris: Block I was declared a national park in 1938 after being a Resident Sportsmen's Shooting Reserve from 1900, while the neighbouring block across the river was the 1900 sanctuary. Several things in the proposal and in the secondary sources were corrected or held apart: the reserve's date (1900 in the IUCN directory and the society's own timeline, 1898 in the society's Wikipedia article); the other early reserve's date (1900 or 1905); the park's date (25 February 1938 for Block I in the IUCN directory, against 1 March 1938, which is the commencement of the Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance No. 2 of 1937 and the date the directory gives for the strict reserve); and the first ranger, Henry Engelbrecht, whom one source has appointed in 1905 and dead in 1922, while his gravestone as transcribed in 2014 gives his death as 25 March 1928 after 21 years' service. The proposal's C006 reading was dropped because the texts do not list killing among the acts greed drives; C006 now refuses the verdict instead of making it. Please judge in particular: whether a third animal film is acceptable in this group, and whether this film and the elephant nursery film (IDEA-0026, proposed) are too close in arc to keep both. The district count for the location's district (named in suggested_location.region) moves from 5 to 6.

suggested_location.name: Yala National Park, Block I (Ruhuna National Park Block I), entered at the Palatupana gate

also_known_as.name: Ruhuna National Park, Block I
also_known_as.meaning: the official name of the park's first block, after the ancient southern kingdom
also_known_as.used_by: Department of Wildlife Conservation; IUCN directory

also_known_as.name: Yala
also_known_as.meaning: the common name for the park, from the old settlement and bungalow at the mouth of the Menik Ganga

also_known_as.name: Resident Sportsmen's Shooting Reserve
also_known_as.meaning: the block's legal status from 1900 until 1938, per the IUCN directory (1990)

suggested_location.region: Hambantota District, Southern Province, on the south-east coast. Block I lies wholly in Hambantota District: the Palatupana gate (6.2764, 81.4030), the Block I node in OpenStreetMap (6.3486, 81.4505), the Thalgasmankada point on the Menik Ganga (6.3972, 81.4845) and the riverbank photographed on Commons (6.3718, 81.5197) all return Hambantota District from OpenStreetMap/Nominatim. The park as a whole spans Southern and Uva provinces (the IUCN directory says so), and the upper Menik Ganga runs through Monaragala District; the film stays inside Block I and on its bank of the river. District count: Hambantota 5 on the slate without GRP-02/03, moves to 6. No other GRP-02 or GRP-03 film is in Hambantota.
suggested_location.why_here: It is the one place on the island where C021's claim, that the drive under any purposeful act takes its colour from what it serves, is a documented fact about a single piece of ground rather than an analogy. This block was reserved by law for resident sportsmen to shoot in from 1900 to 1938, while the sanctuary lay across the river, and since 1938 it has been the national park's first and most frequented block. The reading of tracks, the stillness, the patience and the wish to find the animal are the same on the same ground under both laws; the film performs them with a camera from a halted vehicle and shows, once, that the instrument is rested and steadied the way a rifle is. The place also carries the frame: inselbergs, lagoons, open plain, dry river and heat haze, some of the finest wild country on the island, filmed here in a way it is rarely filmed, through extreme telephoto with no drone.

historical_thread.story: The Ceylon Game Protection Society was formed on 23 May 1894 at a meeting of twenty-six sportsmen at the Bristol Hotel, Colombo, organised by Captain E. Gordon Reeves, with Rear Admiral W. R. Kennedy as honorary president and R. W. Levers, Government Agent of the North Central Province, as chairman (Wikipedia's account of the society; the society's own history of 1931 by A. C. Tutein-Nolthenius, 37 Years of Game Protection in Ceylon, was located by title only). Its first recorded success was a law against the export of, and trade in, hides, horns and dried meat. Its own published timeline says that in 1899 it paid the first game watchers from its own funds, and that in 1900 the government proclaimed the Yala and Wilpattu reserves under the Forest Ordinance 'following constant pressure from the Society'. On 23 March 1900 (the date in the Yala article, citing P. M. Senaratna's 2009 Sinhala book on the national parks) the land between the Menik Ganga and the Kumbukkan Oya, about 389 square kilometres, was made a sanctuary, and the forest between Palatupana and Yala was reserved for resident sportsmen to hunt in. The IUCN Directory of South Asian Protected Areas (1990), citing T. W. Hoffmann's 1969 history of the society in its journal Loris, states it plainly: Block I of Ruhuna National Park was established in 1938, 'having previously been a Resident Sportsmen's Shooting Reserve in 1900', and Block II was 'originally proclaimed as Yala Sanctuary in 1900'. Some years after 1900 the sanctuary was given a ranger, Henry (H. E.) Engelbrecht, an Afrikaner prisoner of war from the camps on the island who refused the oath of allegiance after the South African war and was not repatriated; accounts say he was sent to Hambantota on an allowance and then made Game Sanctuary Ranger, and they describe him as a first-class shot, a good tracker and shikari, words attributed to Leonard Woolf, who was Assistant Government Agent at Hambantota from 1908 to 1911 and whose autobiography Growing (1961) is said to describe him. During the First World War he was arrested on an allegation of supplying the German cruiser Emden and later released. His gravestone, erected by members of the Ceylon Game Protection Society, reads (as transcribed in the Sunday Times in 2014) that he died on 25 March 1928 and was for twenty-one years the guardian of the Yala Game Sanctuary. The Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance, No. 2 of 1937, came into operation on 1 March 1938; it abolished the game sanctuaries of the Forest Ordinance and made national parks, in which all hunting is prohibited. The IUCN directory dates Block I's establishment as a national park to 25 February 1938 and the Yala Strict Natural Reserve to 1 March 1938. Block II followed as national park on 3 September 1954, Blocks III to V in 1967, 1969 and 1973. By 1981 some 100,000 visitors a year came, and the directory notes that Block I 'is most frequented by the public'. The society was renamed the Ceylon Game and Fauna Protection Society in 1930, the Wildlife Protection Society of Ceylon in 1955, and the Wildlife and Nature Protection Society in 1970.
historical_thread.how_it_binds: C021's central finding is that the occasional factors, initial and sustained application, decision, effort, rapture and desire-to-act, are not good or bad in themselves and are counted wholly wholesome or wholly unwholesome by the mind they join [C021-P:L25]; above all, desire-to-act accords with greed in a greed-accompanied mind and opposes it in a mind opposed to greed [C021-M:L27] [C021-P:L75]. A place cannot show a mind. What this place can show, and no other can in the same way, is the same set of working parts running on the same ground under two opposite laws. The record is not an interpretation: an institution of sportsmen drew a line in 1900 that reserved this block for shooting and kept the next for sanctuary, and in 1938 this block became the park that the public now watches more than any other. Its first ranger was, by every account, chosen for his skill as a shot and a tracker. The stalk the camera makes, fixing on a track and staying with it [C021-P:L33] [C021-P:L41] [C021-M:L11], not falling back until the thing begun is done [C021-M:L19], wishing only to find the animal [C021-P:L69], is the stalk the reservation licensed. The history asks the concept's own question, what colour does a drive have, and answers it the way the texts do: the colour is not in the drive. C006 binds because the same history invites a false answer to its question, that the shooting was greed and the watching is not; the Pradeepika's list of the courses of action done through greed does not include killing [C006-P:L54], and the three dials it does examine are not in any gazette [C006-P:L25] [C006-P:L33] [C006-P:L44]. The question of who wrote the story down is part of the film: almost everything known about how this ground was divided comes from the sportsmen's society's own histories (1931 and 1969) and its present-day timeline, which credit its own pressure for the sanctuary and record the shooting reserve beside it without comment.
what_is_certain: The Ceylon Game Protection Society was founded in 1894 (23 May in its Wikipedia article); it is the body now called the Wildlife and Nature Protection Society, and its own timeline gives the names Ceylon Game and Fauna Protection Society (1930), Wildlife Protection Society of Ceylon (1955) and Wildlife and Nature Protection Society (1970).

The IUCN Directory of South Asian Protected Areas (1990) states that Block I of Ruhuna National Park was established in 1938, having previously been a Resident Sportsmen's Shooting Reserve in 1900, and that Block II was originally proclaimed as Yala Sanctuary in 1900. The Yala article, citing Senaratna (2009), agrees: the 1900 reserve lay between the Menik and Kumbukkan rivers, and the forest between Palatupana and Yala was reserved for resident sportsmen to hunt in.

The society's own published timeline says it paid the first game watchers from its funds in 1899 and that the government proclaimed the Yala and Wilpattu reserves under the Forest Ordinance in 1900 'following constant pressure from the Society'.

The Fauna and Flora Protection Ordinance is No. 2 of 1937 and came into operation on 1 March 1938 (FAOLEX; Sri Lanka Biodiversity Clearing House). The IUCN directory says it abolished the Forest Ordinance game sanctuaries.

Block I is 14,102 ha in the IUCN directory (originally 13,680 ha, enlarged in 1968 and 1973) and was the block 'most frequented by the public' when the directory was written; there were about 100,000 visitors in 1981.
Block I lies in Hambantota District: every point checked inside it and at its gate returns Hambantota District from OpenStreetMap/Nominatim.
The landscape: a coastal plain with scattered gneiss inselbergs up to about 90 m, rock pools, freshwater lakes and brackish lagoons (IUCN directory).
Leonard Woolf was Assistant Government Agent of Hambantota District from 1908 to 1911.
what_is_disputed: The year of the first reserve: 1900 (IUCN directory; the society's own timeline; the Yala article, 23 March 1900) against 1898 (the society's Wikipedia article: 'In 1898, through the society's efforts, the Yala Sanctuary ... was gazetted'). Both are kept; the voice says 1900, which is the society's own date and the directory's.

The date of the second early reserve, Wilpattu: 1900 (the society's timeline and the Yala article, both reserves together) against 1905 (the IUCN directory and the society's Wikipedia article). It is not in the film.

The date Block I became a national park: 25 February 1938 (IUCN directory) against 1 March 1938 (the Yala article, which says the ordinance was 'passed' that day). 1 March 1938 is the ordinance's date of commencement and the directory's date for the strict natural reserve, and a park declared under the ordinance six days before it came into operation is odd on its own terms; the gazette was not reached. The voice says only 1938.

Henry Engelbrecht's appointment: 1905 by Governor Sir Henry Blake (AmazingLanka, citing De Costa 1978, Brohier 1947 and Paulier 1947); 'around 1908' by the Government Agent (the Yala article and sites copying it); and, by arithmetic from his gravestone's 'for 21 years' and a death in 1928, about 1907. The voice gives no year.

Engelbrecht's death: 25 March 1922 (AmazingLanka) against 25 March 1928 (his gravestone as transcribed in the Sunday Times, 26 October 2014, and the Sunday Times of 5 July 2026, 'died in 1928 aged 58'). The 1922 date cannot stand with the same source's own appointment year and the gravestone's twenty-one years. The voice says only that the accounts disagree.

Leonard Woolf's Hambantota years: 1908 to 1911 (his own diaries, as used by Thuppahi's blog and most sources) against '1904-1906' (the Sunday Times, 5 July 2026). Woolf reached the island at the end of 1904 and served first in Jaffna, so the second date is wrong. Woolf is not named in the voice.

The society's motive. Its Wikipedia article says its main concern was to curb commercial hunting 'as it was dramatically impacting on their enjoyment as sports hunters'. That sentence is unsourced and attributes a state of mind to identifiable people, so it is not used in the voice in any form. The documented facts are what the society did: it lobbied against the trade in hides, horns and dried meat, paid watchers, and pressed for the reserves.

Whether the river was the exact line between the shooting reserve and the sanctuary along its whole length. Both published accounts place the sanctuary east of the Menik Ganga and the shooting reserve between Palatupana and Yala, which puts the river between them, but the 1900 proclamation and its boundary schedule were not reached.

what_to_film: The track just inside the gate in the early afternoon, at 600 to 800 mm, straight down its length: heat haze, scrub and a distant inselberg stacked into layers. Locked; twenty seconds or more.
Tracks in the sand of the track beside the halted vehicle in raking light, pug marks across wheel ruts, then a slow pan following them into the scrub. The vehicle does not move.

A bird of prey (crested serpent eagle and white-bellied sea eagle are both recorded in the park) taking off with hard wingbeats and then gliding, followed on the long lens. This depends on luck and may need several sessions.

The Menik Ganga in the dry season from its Block I bank, at whichever point the permitted route reaches it: pale sand bed, pools, the forest wall of the far bank (the old sanctuary). Looking across, not along.
A shrinking waterhole in the dry season with deer and buffalo, held for a full minute of screen time with nothing but small movements.
The open plain in late sun with the inselbergs going orange behind it, still on a long lens so that the plain compresses into bands.

The last light on a rock with an animal on it, held for minutes; then the reverse angle from outside the vehicle (a second vehicle or an assistant at the permitted distance, subject to the rules) of the lens resting on a bean bag on the sill. No face or hands in frame.
Sound: heat, insects, peacocks, langurs, the engine only at the very end. No music under the waiting beats.
suggested_location.access: The main public entrance to Block I is the Palatupana gate, reached from Tissamaharama and Kirinda. Entry is by vehicle only on the park's tracks, during the park's opening hours (normally 06:00 to 18:00, with morning and afternoon sessions); visitors must stay in the vehicle except at designated points. Drones are prohibited in national parks, and none is planned. Commercial filming requires a permit from the Department of Wildlife Conservation, which must also clear the reverse-angle shot (a second vehicle or a crew member at the vehicle's side) and the use of a long-lens rig on the sill. Jeep congestion at animal sightings in Block I is a known problem; the film needs quiet stretches and should not join a cluster of vehicles at any sighting. None of this has been checked with the Department.
suggested_location.best_time: Dry season, roughly June to August, in the afternoon session and into the last light before the six o'clock closing. The park normally closes for several weeks from September (dates vary; confirm with the Department each year). Plan several afternoons: the raptor, the tracks and the final animal all depend on luck.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, 2026-09-26. The load-bearing fact (Block I was the Resident Sportsmen's Shooting Reserve from 1900 and became a national park in 1938; the 1900 sanctuary was Block II) was read in the full text of the IUCN Directory of South Asian Protected Areas (Green, 1990) on archive.org, and in the archived IWMI wetland profile of Ruhuna, which repeats it; the directory cites T. W. Hoffmann (1969), 'The Wildlife Protection Society of Ceylon: some historical reflections on the occasion of its 75th anniversary', Loris 11: 1-13, which was not reached. The earliest attestation actually reached is therefore 1990, resting on the society's own 1969 history; the society's 1931 history (Tutein-Nolthenius) was located by title only, and the 1900 proclamation and its boundary schedule were not found. Everything about Henry Engelbrecht is secondary (newspaper features and a heritage site, citing De Costa 1978, Brohier 1947 and Paulier 1947); Woolf's Growing could not be read (the archive.org copies are lending-only), so the 'first-class shot, good tracker and shikari' description is attributed in the voice to 'the accounts', not to Woolf. Corrections to the blind proposal: Wilpattu's reserve is 1900 or 1905, not simply 1900; the 1938 date is 25 February for Block I in the directory, with 1 March the ordinance's commencement; Engelbrecht's appointment is 1905, c. 1907 or c. 1908 depending on the source, not simply 1908; the proposal's C006 reading was doctrinally unsafe (the texts do not list killing among the acts of greed) and was replaced. The Wikipedia claim that a Spanish cartographer's map of 1560 described Yala as abandoned for 300 years was not used; it looks like the kind of repeated, unsourced figure the method warns about. District: Hambantota moves from 5 to 6, which is above the preferred 4 but below the cap; it was accepted because the story exists only in this block. Coordinates are the OpenStreetMap node for Block I; the gate is at 6.2764, 81.4030. Images: three Commons files confirmed by the imageinfo API; the river photograph is georeferenced inside Block I; the Elephant Rock file carries a GPS tag outside the park and is captioned accordingly. The 2004 tsunami site on this block's shore, Engelbrecht's grave in Hambantota and the seasonal fishing camp are deliberately excluded. No access, permit or filming condition has been checked with the Department of Wildlife Conservation.

evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. The location was proposed by Claude and awaits Chathura's review; it has not been confirmed. The shooting-reserve history is documentary at one remove (the IUCN directory of 1990, citing the society's 1969 history) and is corroborated by the society's own published timeline and by a 2009 Sinhala book cited in Wikipedia; the ordinance's number and commencement date are from legal databases; the account of Henry Engelbrecht is journalism and heritage writing citing earlier secondary works, and its dates conflict; the district was checked by reverse geocoding. Access, permissions and filming conditions are desk research and unverified. No scene or shot has been filmed.
